newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bradford signals S.I. power differential may go.
newsitem.headline: Bradford signals S.I. power differential may go.

text.p: Energy Minister Max Bradford signalled little support on Wednesday for those favouring retaining the South Island electricity differential, saying lower prices in the South Island already reflected lower transmission costs there.
Bradford is to decide in the next few days if the South Island electricity differential will continue.
South Island MPs and South Island power companies argue the differential is needed because the electricity market in the South Island is not working properly.
South Islanders believe they should have cheaper electricity than North Islanders because of their proximity to the hydro generators.

But Bradford, in a speech to the electricity industry, said one of the aims of the electricity reforms was to see that consumers paid the true cost of transmission and generation of their electricity.
"An example of this can be seen in the prices paid by South Island consumers," he said.

"Since the market came into effect in October last year the combined spot prices and long term contracts have delivered an estimated average differential of about eight to nine percent in favour of South Island consumers.
"This excludes the effect of the NZ$10.9 million government subsidy whose future has gained so much attention recently," Bradford said, referring to the differential.
"In other words, the market is delivering competitive power prices which recognise the lower costs of transmission and generation in the South Island," he said.

Labour energy spokesman Pete Hodgson released figures on Wednesday showing last week's market differential had fallen to 0.07 percent. It was the lowest level since the market began in October, he said.
Hodgson said for the week ending Sunday night, the South Island reference point wholesale price was 5.787 cents whereas the North Island reference point price was 5.791 cents.
"In other words the market difference has dwindled to 0.004 cents per unit, justifying my prediction in April that the differential would evaporate altogether in winter."
Hodgson said the government had to think again about the argument presented by South Island MPs that the wholesale electricity market was not reliably delivering a differential.

"The reason is that electricity actually runs southwards during the winter evenings as North Island thermal electricity is used to conserve South Island lakes. This actually creates an overnight differential in favour of the North Island," he said.
But it was the daytime use of South Island hydro in the North Island that created the need for back-loading overnight.
The "strange economic model" used meant night-time electricity consumed in the South Island had to be delivered from the North Island because it had been sold north only hours earlier, Hodgson said.
